goals: Describe the organisation of the human neural system
Describe the structure and types of neurons
Explain the resting potential, the action potential and conduction of a nerve impulse
Explain transmission of impulses across electrical and chemical synapses

slides.heading: Neural Control and Coordination
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how the neural system is organised, and how neurons generate and pass on impulses.

visual.alt: Flow from a stimulus through receptors and the central neural system to effectors

slides.narration: Coordination is the process through which two or more organs interact and complement each other’s functions. During exercise, for example, muscles need more oxygen, so breathing, heart rate and blood flow all rise together. The neural system and the endocrine system jointly coordinate and integrate the activities of the organs. The neural system gives an organised network of point to point connections for quick coordination.

slides.heading: The human neural system
slides.body_md: The **central neural system (CNS)** includes the **brain and the spinal cord** and is the site of information processing and control. The **peripheral neural system (PNS)** has all the nerves associated with the CNS.

rows: Carry impulses from tissues and organs to the CNS
Carry regulatory impulses from the CNS to the peripheral tissues and organs
Relays impulses from the CNS to skeletal muscles
Relays impulses from the CNS to the involuntary organs and smooth muscles; divided into sympathetic and parasympathetic
Part of the PNS: nerves, fibres, ganglia and plexuses carrying impulses between the CNS and the viscera

visual.alt: Table of the divisions of the peripheral neural system

slides.narration: Afferent fibres bring messages in to the brain and spinal cord; efferent fibres carry orders out. The somatic system works our skeletal muscles. The autonomic system, with its sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions, runs the involuntary organs and smooth muscles.

slides.heading: The neuron
slides.body_md: A **neuron** is a microscopic structure made of three major parts: the **cell body**, **dendrites** and the **axon**. The cell body contains cytoplasm with typical organelles and granular **Nissl’s granules**. Short, repeatedly branched **dendrites** (which also contain Nissl’s granules) carry impulses **towards** the cell body. The **axon** is a long fibre whose distal end is branched; each branch ends as a bulb-like **synaptic knob** containing **synaptic vesicles** with **neurotransmitters**. Axons carry impulses **away** from the cell body to a synapse or a neuromuscular junction.

slides.narration: Dendrites are the receiving branches, the cell body is the control centre with its nucleus and Nissl’s granules, and the axon is the long sending cable. In a myelinated axon, Schwann cells wrap a myelin sheath around the axon, leaving small gaps called the nodes of Ranvier.

slides.heading: Kinds of neurons and nerve fibres
slides.body_md: Neurons are classified by the number of axons and dendrites; axons are **myelinated** or **non-myelinated**.

slides.heading: The resting membrane
slides.body_md: Ion channels in the axonal membrane are selectively permeable. At rest the membrane is **more permeable to K⁺** and **nearly impermeable to Na⁺**, and impermeable to the negatively charged proteins of the axoplasm. The axoplasm has a **high K⁺** and **low Na⁺** concentration; the fluid outside has **low K⁺** and **high Na⁺**. The **sodium–potassium pump** transports **3 Na⁺ outwards for 2 K⁺ into the cell**. The outer surface is positive and the inner surface negative: the membrane is **polarised**, and the potential difference is the **resting potential**.

slides.narration: At rest, the axon keeps sodium mostly outside and potassium mostly inside. The pump moves three sodium ions out for every two potassium ions it brings in, so the outside stays positive and the inside negative. This charge difference across the membrane is the resting potential.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: counting the pump
slides.body_md: A patch of axonal membrane completes 200 cycles of the sodium–potassium pump. How many Na⁺ ions leave, how many K⁺ ions enter, and how many positive charges are moved out overall?
bullets: Na⁺ out: $3 \times 200 = 600$.
Net positive charges moved out: $600 - 400 = 200$, one per cycle.
The pump therefore helps keep the outside of the membrane positive with respect to the inside.

visual.alt: Worked table: 200 pump cycles move 600 sodium out and 400 potassium in

slides.narration: Each cycle sends three sodium ions out and brings two potassium ions in. So two hundred cycles move six hundred sodium out and four hundred potassium in, a net loss of two hundred positive charges from the inside. That is why the pump helps keep the inside negative.

slides.heading: The action potential
slides.body_md: When a **stimulus** is applied at a site on the polarised membrane, the membrane there becomes **freely permeable to Na⁺**. A rapid **influx of Na⁺** reverses the polarity: the outer surface becomes negative and the inner surface positive, so the site is **depolarised**. The electrical potential difference across the membrane at that site is the **action potential**, which is in fact termed a **nerve impulse**. The rise in Na⁺ permeability is extremely short-lived; it is quickly followed by a rise in **K⁺ permeability**, K⁺ diffuses out, and the resting potential is restored (**repolarisation**). Typical values: about -70 mV at rest and about +30 mV at the peak.

slides.narration: A stimulus opens the way for sodium ions to flood in, and for a moment the inside of the membrane becomes positive. Almost at once, potassium ions flow out and the membrane returns to its resting state, ready to respond to a further stimulation. The voltages shown are typical values, not exact figures for every neuron.

slides.heading: Conduction along the axon
slides.body_md: At the depolarised site A, the inner surface is positive while the adjacent site B is still negative inside. **Current flows on the inner surface from A to B**, and on the outer surface from B to A, completing a circuit. Site B is then depolarised and an action potential is generated there, while site A repolarises. The sequence repeats along the length of the axon, so the **impulse is conducted**.

nodes.label: Current flows from A to B

visual.alt: Flow of an impulse spreading from site A to site B along an axon

slides.narration: Think of a line of falling dominoes that stand themselves back up. Each depolarised patch makes local currents flow to the patch next door, which then fires, while the first patch recovers. In this way the impulse travels along the whole axon.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: how long does an impulse take?
slides.body_md: An impulse travels 0.8 m along a myelinated fibre at 50 m per second, and the same distance along a non-myelinated fibre at 1 m per second (typical illustrative speeds). Find each time in milliseconds and compare.
bullets: Myelinated: $\dfrac{0.8}{50} \times 1000 = 16$ ms.
Non-myelinated: $\dfrac{0.8}{1} \times 1000 = 800$ ms.
Ratio: $\dfrac{800}{16} = 50$, so the myelinated fibre is 50 times faster here.
Speeds vary widely with the fibre; myelinated fibres conduct much faster than non-myelinated fibres of similar size.

visual.alt: Worked table: 16 milliseconds against 800 milliseconds

slides.narration: Time is distance divided by speed. Point eight metres at fifty metres a second takes sixteen milliseconds, but at one metre a second it takes eight hundred milliseconds, fifty times as long. The speeds are only typical values chosen for the example.

slides.heading: The synapse
slides.body_md: A nerve impulse is transmitted from one neuron to another through junctions called **synapses**. A synapse is formed by the membranes of a **pre-synaptic** neuron and a **post-synaptic** neuron, which may or may not be separated by a gap called the **synaptic cleft**. At a **chemical synapse**, an impulse arriving at the axon terminal stimulates the movement of the synaptic vesicles towards the membrane, where they fuse and release **neurotransmitters** into the cleft. These bind to specific **receptors** on the post-synaptic membrane, opening **ion channels**; the entry of ions can generate a **new potential**, which may be **excitatory or inhibitory**.

slides.narration: At a chemical synapse the message changes from electrical to chemical and back. The impulse releases neurotransmitter from vesicles, the molecules cross the fluid-filled cleft, bind to receptors and open ion channels, and a new potential may start in the next neuron.

slides.heading: Electrical and chemical synapses
slides.body_md: There are two types of synapses.

rows: Pre- and post-synaptic membranes in very close proximity
Separated by a fluid-filled synaptic cleft
Electric current flows directly from one neuron into the other
Neurotransmitters released into the cleft bind to receptors
Always faster; similar to conduction along a single axon

visual.alt: Table comparing electrical and chemical synapses

slides.narration: Electrical synapses pass current straight across from one neuron to the next, so they are very fast, but they are rare in our system. Most of our synapses are chemical, using neurotransmitters to carry the signal across the cleft.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: CNS: brain and spinal cord; PNS: afferent and efferent fibres; somatic and autonomic (sympathetic, parasympathetic); visceral nervous system.
Neuron: cell body with Nissl’s granules, dendrites (towards), axon (away) ending in synaptic knobs; multipolar, bipolar, unipolar.
Myelinated fibres (Schwann cells, nodes of Ranvier) in spinal and cranial nerves; non-myelinated in autonomous and somatic systems.
Resting: more permeable to K⁺; pump 3 Na⁺ out for 2 K⁺ in; outside positive, inside negative (polarised).
Stimulus: Na⁺ influx, depolarisation, action potential; K⁺ out, repolarisation; local currents conduct the impulse.
Synapses: electrical (direct current, faster, rare) and chemical (neurotransmitter, receptors, ion channels; excitatory or inhibitory).

visual.alt: Summary table of membrane charge in three states

slides.narration: To recap: neurons receive signals on dendrites and send them along axons. At rest the membrane is polarised. A stimulus lets sodium rush in, producing an action potential, and potassium flowing out restores the resting state. Impulses pass to the next cell across electrical or chemical synapses.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Draw and label a **myelinated neuron**: dendrites, cell body, Nissl’s granules, axon, myelin sheath, node of Ranvier, synaptic knob.
State the **ion distribution** and the **3 : 2 pump** for the resting potential.
Explain **depolarisation** (Na⁺ in) and **repolarisation** (K⁺ out) in order.
Describe **chemical transmission** step by step: vesicles, cleft, receptors, ion channels.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Practise a labelled neuron. Learn which ion is high on each side and how the pump keeps it so. Explain depolarisation and repolarisation in the right order. And describe each step of transmission at a chemical synapse.

decks.title: Neural Control and Coordination — Part 2: The brain and reflex action
goals: Describe how the brain is protected
Describe the parts and functions of the forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain
Explain reflex action and the reflex arc, using the knee jerk

slides.heading: The central neural system
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the brain, the central information-processing organ, and the reflex arcs of the spinal cord.

visual.alt: Flow from forebrain through midbrain and hindbrain to the spinal cord

slides.narration: The brain is the central information processing organ of the body and acts as the command and control system. It controls voluntary movements, the balance of the body, the functioning of vital involuntary organs such as the lungs, heart and kidneys, thermoregulation, hunger and thirst, circadian rhythms, the activities of several endocrine glands, and human behaviour. It is also the site for processing of vision, hearing, speech, memory, intelligence, emotions and thoughts.

slides.heading: Protection of the brain
slides.body_md: The human brain is well protected by the **skull**. Inside the skull, the brain is covered by **cranial meninges**, three layers.

rows: Inner layer, in contact with the brain tissue

visual.alt: Table of the three cranial meninges from outside in

slides.narration: Outside, the hard skull guards the brain. Underneath lie three membranes: the tough dura mater on the outside, the very thin arachnoid in the middle, and the pia mater, which clings to the surface of the brain itself.

slides.heading: The brain in section
slides.body_md: The brain can be divided into three major parts: the **forebrain**, the **midbrain** and the **hindbrain**.

slides.narration: Look first at the big cerebrum on top, joined across the middle by the corpus callosum. Deep inside sit the thalamus and, below it, the hypothalamus. The short midbrain links up to the pons, the cerebellum lies behind, and the medulla continues down into the spinal cord.

slides.heading: Forebrain: the cerebrum
slides.body_md: The forebrain consists of the **cerebrum**, **thalamus** and **hypothalamus**. A deep cleft divides the cerebrum longitudinally into **left and right cerebral hemispheres**, connected by a tract of nerve fibres, the **corpus callosum**.

rows: Layer of cells covering the hemispheres, thrown into prominent folds; called grey matter because neuron cell bodies are concentrated here
Motor areas, sensory areas, association areas
The cortex contains motor and sensory areas, and large regions that are neither, the association areas, responsible for complex functions such as intersensory associations, memory and communication
Fibres of the tracts, covered with a myelin sheath, form the inner part of the cerebral hemisphere and give it an opaque white appearance

visual.alt: Table of the parts of the cerebrum

slides.narration: The cerebrum forms the major part of the human brain. Its folded grey cortex holds the cell bodies of neurons, with motor, sensory and association areas. Beneath lies white matter, made of myelinated fibres, which links regions together.

slides.heading: Thalamus, hypothalamus and limbic system
slides.body_md: The cerebrum wraps around the thalamus, the hypothalamus and the inner parts of the cerebral hemispheres.

rows: A major coordinating centre for sensory and motor signalling
At the base of the thalamus; contains centres that control body temperature and the urge for eating and drinking; groups of neurosecretory cells secrete hypothalamic hormones
Limbic system (amygdala, hippocampus and other inner parts)
Along with the hypothalamus, involved in the regulation of sexual behaviour, expression of emotional reactions such as excitement, pleasure, rage and fear, and motivation

visual.alt: Table of the thalamus, hypothalamus and limbic system

slides.narration: The thalamus is a relay and coordinating centre for sensory and motor signals. The hypothalamus, just below it, controls body temperature, hunger and thirst, and makes hormones. Inner parts of the hemispheres, such as the amygdala and hippocampus, form the limbic system, which with the hypothalamus shapes emotions, sexual behaviour and motivation.

slides.heading: Quick check: hypothalamus
slides.body_md: Which part of the forebrain contains centres that control body temperature and the urge for eating and drinking?
slides.narration: Quick check. It lies at the base of the thalamus.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: which region is affected?
slides.body_md: Use the functions of brain regions to work out the part most likely affected in each person.
bullets: A person whose body temperature swings wildly and who never feels thirsty → **hypothalamus** (centres for body temperature, eating and drinking).
A patient whose breathing and heart rate become irregular after an injury at the base of the brain → **medulla** (respiration and cardiovascular reflexes).
A patient in whom signals cannot pass between the left and right cerebral hemispheres → **corpus callosum** (tract joining the hemispheres).
A person showing unusual rage and fear after damage deep in the hemispheres → **limbic system** (amygdala, hippocampus).

visual.alt: Worked table matching four signs with the brain regions responsible

slides.narration: Match each sign with a known function. Temperature and thirst point to the hypothalamus. Breathing and heart rhythm point to the medulla. Two hemispheres unable to share information point to the corpus callosum. And changes in emotional reactions point to the limbic system.

slides.heading: Midbrain and hindbrain
slides.body_md: The **midbrain** lies between the thalamus or hypothalamus of the forebrain and the pons of the hindbrain. A canal, the **cerebral aqueduct**, passes through it. Its dorsal portion has mainly four round swellings called the **corpora quadrigemina**. The **hindbrain** comprises the **pons**, **cerebellum** and **medulla** (medulla oblongata).

rows: Fibre tracts that interconnect different regions of the brain
Very convoluted surface, giving additional space for many more neurons
Connected to the spinal cord; centres control respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretions
Midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata; connects the brain to the spinal cord

visual.alt: Table of the parts of the hindbrain and the brain stem

slides.narration: The midbrain carries the cerebral aqueduct and the four swellings of the corpora quadrigemina on its back. In the hindbrain, the pons links brain regions together, the much folded cerebellum packs in a great many neurons, and the medulla runs breathing, heart and gut reflexes. Midbrain, pons and medulla together make the brain stem.

slides.heading: Quick check: brain stem
slides.body_md: Which three parts form the brain stem?
slides.narration: Quick check. The brain stem links the brain to the spinal cord.

slides.heading: The reflex arc
slides.body_md: The entire process of response to a peripheral nervous stimulation that occurs **involuntarily**, without conscious effort or thought and requiring the involvement of a part of the central nervous system, is called a **reflex action**. The reflex pathway comprises at least one **afferent neuron** (receptor) and one **efferent** (effector or excitor) **neuron** appropriately arranged in a series.

slides.narration: In the knee jerk, a tap below the knee cap stretches the thigh muscle. The afferent neuron carries the signal through the dorsal nerve root into the spinal cord. There it passes directly to an efferent neuron, which carries the signal back to the muscle, and the leg kicks out.

slides.heading: Steps of a reflex action
slides.body_md: The afferent neuron receives the signal from a sensory organ and transmits the impulse via a **dorsal nerve root** into the CNS (at the level of the spinal cord). The efferent neuron then carries signals from the CNS to the **effector**. The stimulus and response thus form a **reflex arc**.

visual.alt: Flow of a reflex arc from stimulus to effector

slides.narration: Every reflex follows the same path: a stimulus, a receptor, an afferent neuron into the spinal cord, an efferent neuron out, and an effector that responds. Because the signal need not travel up to the cerebrum and back, the response is quick and automatic.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: timing a knee jerk
slides.body_md: In a knee jerk, the afferent and efferent neurons are each about 0.9 m long and conduct at 90 m per second, and the single synapse in the spinal cord adds a delay of 0.5 ms (typical illustrative values). Estimate the reflex time.
bullets: Afferent: $\dfrac{0.9}{90} \times 1000 = 10$ ms.
Efferent: $\dfrac{0.9}{90} \times 1000 = 10$ ms.
Only one synapse is crossed, so the reflex is very quick.

visual.alt: Worked table: the knee jerk takes about 20.5 milliseconds

slides.narration: Each neuron carries the signal nought point nine metres at ninety metres a second, which takes ten milliseconds. Add the half millisecond delay at the synapse and the total is about twenty and a half milliseconds, far quicker than a response that has to be thought about.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Protection: skull and cranial meninges (dura mater, arachnoid, pia mater).
Forebrain: cerebrum (hemispheres, corpus callosum, cortex as grey matter with motor, sensory and association areas, white matter), thalamus, hypothalamus, limbic system (amygdala, hippocampus).
Midbrain: cerebral aqueduct, corpora quadrigemina. Hindbrain: pons, cerebellum, medulla. Brain stem: midbrain, pons, medulla.
Reflex action: involuntary response; reflex arc of receptor, afferent neuron (dorsal root), CNS, efferent neuron, effector; knee jerk.

visual.alt: Summary table of key brain regions and roles

slides.narration: To recap: the brain is guarded by the skull and three meninges. The forebrain thinks, senses and controls drives; the midbrain and hindbrain relay signals and run vital reflexes. And reflex arcs through the spinal cord give fast, automatic responses such as the knee jerk.

sections.heading: 1. Neural system, neuron, nerve impulse and synapse
sections.body_md:
**Coordination** is the process through which two or more organs interact and complement the functions of one another; during physical exercise, for example, the rise in energy demand is matched by increases in breathing, heart rate and blood flow. The **neural system** and the **endocrine system** jointly coordinate and integrate the activities of the organs; the neural system gives an organised network of point-to-point connections for quick coordination.

**Organisation.** The **central neural system (CNS)** includes the **brain and spinal cord** and is the site of information processing and control. The **peripheral neural system (PNS)** comprises all the nerves of the body associated with the CNS. Its nerve fibres are of two types: **afferent fibres** transmit impulses from tissues and organs to the CNS, and **efferent fibres** transmit regulatory impulses from the CNS to the peripheral tissues and organs. The PNS is divided into the **somatic neural system**, which relays impulses from the CNS to **skeletal muscles**, and the **autonomic neural system**, which transmits impulses from the CNS to the **involuntary organs and smooth muscles**; the autonomic system is further classified into the **sympathetic** and **parasympathetic** neural systems. The **visceral nervous system** is the part of the PNS comprising the whole complex of nerves, fibres, ganglia and plexuses by which impulses travel from the CNS to the viscera and from the viscera to the CNS.

**Neuron.** A neuron has a **cell body** (cytoplasm, organelles and **Nissl’s granules**), **dendrites** (short, repeatedly branched fibres, also with Nissl’s granules, carrying impulses **towards** the cell body) and an **axon** (a long fibre whose distal end is branched, each branch ending in a bulb-like **synaptic knob** with **synaptic vesicles** containing **neurotransmitters**; axons carry impulses **away** from the cell body to a synapse or a neuromuscular junction).
- **Multipolar** (one axon, two or more dendrites): cerebral cortex. **Bipolar** (one axon, one dendrite): retina of the eye. **Unipolar** (cell body with one axon only): usually found in the embryonic stage.
- **Myelinated** fibres are enveloped by **Schwann cells** forming a **myelin sheath** around the axon; the gaps between adjacent sheaths are the **nodes of Ranvier**; they occur in spinal and cranial nerves. **Unmyelinated** fibres are enclosed by a Schwann cell that does not form a myelin sheath; they are commonly found in the autonomous and the somatic neural systems.

**Resting potential.** Neurons are excitable cells because their membranes are polarised. Ion channels are selectively permeable. At rest the axonal membrane is **more permeable to K⁺**, **nearly impermeable to Na⁺**, and impermeable to the negatively charged proteins of the axoplasm. The axoplasm contains a **high K⁺**, negatively charged proteins and **low Na⁺**; the fluid outside has **low K⁺** and **high Na⁺**. These gradients are maintained by the **sodium–potassium pump**, which transports **3 Na⁺ outwards for 2 K⁺ into the cell**. The outer surface is therefore **positive** and the inner surface **negative**: the membrane is **polarised**, and the electrical potential difference across it is the **resting potential** (typically about -70 mV).

**Action potential and conduction.** When a stimulus is applied at a site (say A), the membrane there becomes **freely permeable to Na⁺**; a rapid **influx of Na⁺** reverses the polarity, making the outer surface negative and the inner surface positive (**depolarisation**). This potential difference is the **action potential**, also termed a **nerve impulse** (typically peaking at about +30 mV). At the adjacent site B the inner surface is still negative, so **current flows on the inner surface from A to B** and on the outer surface from B to A, completing a circuit; B is depolarised and an action potential is generated there. The sequence repeats along the axon, conducting the impulse. The rise in Na⁺ permeability is extremely short-lived; it is quickly followed by a rise in **K⁺ permeability**, K⁺ diffuses outside, and the resting potential is restored (**repolarisation**), so the fibre becomes ready to respond to further stimulation.

**Synapses.** A synapse is formed by the membranes of a **pre-synaptic** and a **post-synaptic** neuron, which may or may not be separated by a gap called the **synaptic cleft**.
- **Electrical synapses:** the membranes are in very close proximity; electric current flows directly from one neuron into the other; transmission is very similar to conduction along a single axon and is **always faster** than across a chemical synapse; they are **rare** in our system.
- **Chemical synapses:** the membranes are separated by a fluid-filled **synaptic cleft**. **Neurotransmitters** are involved. An impulse arriving at the axon terminal stimulates the synaptic vesicles to move to the plasma membrane, fuse with it and release neurotransmitters into the cleft. They bind to specific **receptors** on the post-synaptic membrane; the binding opens **ion channels**, allowing ions to enter, which can generate a **new potential** in the post-synaptic neuron. The new potential may be **excitatory or inhibitory**.

Gaps between adjacent myelin sheaths on a myelinated axon.

The reversed potential difference at a depolarised site of the membrane; the nerve impulse.
The fluid-filled gap between pre- and post-synaptic membranes at a chemical synapse.

sections.heading: 2. Central neural system: the brain
sections.body_md:
The **brain** is the central information-processing organ and the command and control system. It controls voluntary movements, the balance of the body, the functioning of vital involuntary organs (lungs, heart, kidneys), thermoregulation, hunger and thirst, circadian (24-hour) rhythms, the activities of several endocrine glands and human behaviour, and it is the site of processing of vision, hearing, speech, memory, intelligence, emotions and thoughts.

**Protection.** The brain is protected by the **skull**. Inside the skull it is covered by the **cranial meninges**: an outer **dura mater**, a very thin middle **arachnoid**, and an inner **pia mater** in contact with the brain tissue.

**Forebrain** — cerebrum, thalamus and hypothalamus.
- The **cerebrum** forms the major part of the brain. A deep cleft divides it longitudinally into **left and right cerebral hemispheres**, connected by a tract of nerve fibres, the **corpus callosum**. The layer of cells covering the hemispheres, the **cerebral cortex**, is thrown into prominent folds; it is called **grey matter** because neuron cell bodies are concentrated there. The cortex contains **motor areas**, **sensory areas** and large regions that are neither, the **association areas**, responsible for complex functions such as intersensory associations, memory and communication. Fibres of the tracts, covered with a myelin sheath, form the inner part of the hemisphere and give it an opaque white appearance (**white matter**).
- The cerebrum wraps around the **thalamus**, a major coordinating centre for sensory and motor signalling.
- The **hypothalamus**, at the base of the thalamus, contains centres that control **body temperature** and the **urge for eating and drinking**; it also contains groups of neurosecretory cells that secrete **hypothalamic hormones**.
- The inner parts of the cerebral hemispheres and a group of associated deep structures such as the **amygdala** and **hippocampus** form the **limbic system** (limbic lobe), which, along with the hypothalamus, is involved in the regulation of sexual behaviour, the expression of emotional reactions (excitement, pleasure, rage, fear) and motivation.

**Midbrain** — between the thalamus or hypothalamus of the forebrain and the pons of the hindbrain. A canal, the **cerebral aqueduct**, passes through it. Its dorsal portion consists mainly of four round swellings (lobes) called the **corpora quadrigemina**.

**Hindbrain** — **pons**, **cerebellum** and **medulla** (medulla oblongata).
- The **pons** consists of fibre tracts that interconnect different regions of the brain.
- The **cerebellum** has a very convoluted surface, providing additional space for many more neurons.
- The **medulla** is connected to the spinal cord and contains centres that control **respiration**, **cardiovascular reflexes** and **gastric secretions**.

The **midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata** form the **brain stem**, which forms the connection between the brain and the spinal cord.

sections.heading: 3. Reflex action and reflex arc
sections.body_md:
The entire process of response to a peripheral nervous stimulation that occurs **involuntarily**, i.e., without conscious effort or thought and requiring the involvement of a part of the central nervous system, is called a **reflex action**. The reflex pathway comprises **at least one afferent neuron** (receptor) and **one efferent** (effector or excitor) neuron appropriately arranged in a series.

The **afferent neuron** receives the signal from a sensory organ and transmits the impulse via a **dorsal nerve root** into the CNS (at the level of the spinal cord). The **efferent neuron** then carries signals from the CNS to the **effector**. The stimulus and response thus form a **reflex arc**, as in the **knee jerk reflex**: a tap below the knee cap stretches the thigh muscle; the afferent neuron carries the impulse into the grey matter of the spinal cord, where it passes across a synapse to an efferent neuron, which carries it back to the thigh muscle; the muscle contracts and the leg kicks forward.

Because the impulse need not travel to the brain and back, reflexes are fast and automatic. (With typical illustrative values, two neurons of about 0.9 m conducting at 90 m per second and one synapse delay of 0.5 ms give a knee-jerk time of about 20.5 ms.)

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying dendrites carry impulses away from the cell body (they carry them towards it; the axon carries them away).
- Reversing the charges: at rest the outside is positive and the inside negative.
- Writing that the pump moves 2 Na⁺ out and 3 K⁺ in (it is 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in).
- Saying depolarisation is caused by K⁺ entering (Na⁺ rushes in; K⁺ moves out during repolarisation).
- Calling the cerebral cortex white matter (it is grey matter; the myelinated fibres inside form white matter).
- Putting the pons or medulla in the forebrain, or leaving the midbrain out of the brain stem.
- Saying the brain controls a reflex action consciously.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: name a part of a neuron, a meninx, a brain region or the ion involved in a phase.
- 2–3-mark answers: types of neurons; myelinated and non-myelinated fibres; resting potential; chemical synapse; functions of forebrain parts; reflex arc.
- 5-mark answers: generation and conduction of a nerve impulse; structure and functions of the brain; reflex action with a labelled arc.
- Case-based items: axon recordings, a toxin at a synapse, a head injury, or a knee-jerk test, with a 2-mark part with an internal choice.

questions.stem_md: The central neural system of a human consists of

options.text_md: the brain and the cranial nerves
the brain and the spinal cord
the spinal cord and the spinal nerves
all the nerves associated with the brain

questions.solution_md: The CNS includes the brain and spinal cord; the nerves associated with them form the PNS — option (b).

questions.stem_md: When you touch an ice cube, which nerve fibres carry the message from the skin to the spinal cord?

options.text_md: Fibres of the autonomic system going to smooth muscle

questions.solution_md: Afferent fibres transmit impulses from tissues and organs to the CNS — option (d).

questions.stem_md: When a dog suddenly barks behind you, your heart races and the muscles of your gut wall slow down, without any decision on your part. Which part of the peripheral neural system relays these impulses to the involuntary organs and smooth muscles?

options.text_md: The afferent fibres of the skin

questions.solution_md: The autonomic neural system transmits impulses from the CNS to the involuntary organs and smooth muscles; the somatic system serves skeletal muscles — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The whole complex of nerves, fibres, ganglia and plexuses by which impulses travel from the CNS to the viscera and back is called the
questions.solution_md: This part of the PNS is the visceral nervous system — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A stained neuron seen under a microscope shows dark granular bodies in its cell body and in its short branched processes, but none in its long process. Identify the granules and the short processes.

options.text_md: Synaptic vesicles; the short processes are axons
Nissl’s granules; the short processes are dendrites
Nodes of Ranvier; the short processes are Schwann cells
Myelin; the short processes are synaptic knobs

questions.solution_md: The cell body contains granular bodies called Nissl’s granules, and the short, repeatedly branched dendrites also contain them; the long axon does not — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A neuron with one axon and one dendrite is described as
questions.solution_md: Bipolar neurons have one axon and one dendrite, as in the retina of the eye — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A histology slide of a spinal nerve shows axons wrapped in a sheath with regular gaps. The sheath and the gaps are

options.text_md: a sarcolemma formed by muscle cells, with Z lines between them
a pia mater formed by the arachnoid, with synaptic clefts between them
Nissl’s granules, with synaptic knobs between them
a myelin sheath formed by Schwann cells, with nodes of Ranvier between sheaths

questions.solution_md: Myelinated fibres, as in spinal and cranial nerves, are enveloped by Schwann cells forming a myelin sheath; the gaps are nodes of Ranvier — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A neuroscientist studying a cell from the cerebral cortex finds that it has one axon and many dendrites. The cell is
questions.solution_md: One axon with two or more dendrites makes a multipolar neuron, found in the cerebral cortex — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which statement correctly describes a resting (polarised) axonal membrane?

options.text_md: It is freely permeable to Na⁺, and its inner surface is positive.
It is equally permeable to all ions, and both surfaces carry the same charge.
It is impermeable to K⁺, and its outer surface is negative.
It is more permeable to K⁺ than to Na⁺, and its outer surface is positive with respect to the inner surface.

questions.solution_md: At rest the membrane is more permeable to K⁺ and nearly impermeable to Na⁺; the outer surface is positive and the inner negative — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In a short interval, the sodium–potassium pumps on a tiny patch of axon move 30 sodium ions out of the cell. How many potassium ions do they bring in during the same interval?
questions.solution_md: The pump transports 3 Na⁺ outwards for 2 K⁺ inwards, so 30 Na⁺ out goes with 20 K⁺ in — option (a).

questions.stem_md: When a stimulus is applied at a site on a polarised axon, the membrane at that site becomes freely permeable to

options.text_md: K⁺, which rushes in and makes the inside more negative
negatively charged proteins, which leave the axoplasm
Cl⁻ only, which leaves the axon
Na⁺, which rushes in and reverses the polarity

questions.solution_md: The membrane becomes freely permeable to Na⁺; a rapid influx of Na⁺ makes the inner surface positive (depolarisation) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A drug prevents the rise in K⁺ permeability that normally follows the peak of an action potential. Which event will be delayed?

options.text_md: Repolarisation, the return of the membrane to the resting potential

questions.solution_md: The resting potential is restored when K⁺ permeability rises and K⁺ diffuses out; blocking this delays repolarisation — option (b).

questions.stem_md: An isolated axon is placed in a bathing fluid that contains almost no Na⁺ and is then stimulated. What is the most likely result?

options.text_md: No action potential develops, because there is no Na⁺ to rush in and depolarise the membrane.
A larger action potential develops, because K⁺ rushes in instead.
The impulse travels faster than normal.

questions.solution_md: Depolarisation depends on a rapid influx of Na⁺ from outside; without Na⁺ outside, the polarity cannot reverse — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Site A of an axon is depolarised while the next site B is still at rest. In which direction does current flow on the inner surface of the membrane?

options.text_md: Across the membrane from outside to inside only
No current flows until B is stimulated from outside

questions.solution_md: On the inner surface, current flows from the positive site A to the negative site B, and on the outer surface from B to A — option (c).

questions.stem_md: At a chemical synapse, the signal is carried across the synaptic cleft by

options.text_md: an electric current flowing directly between the membranes
Schwann cells moving across the gap
neurotransmitter molecules released from synaptic vesicles
K⁺ ions pumped out of the post-synaptic neuron

questions.solution_md: Synaptic vesicles release neurotransmitters into the cleft; these bind receptors on the post-synaptic membrane — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A plant toxin occupies the receptors on the post-synaptic membrane without opening any ion channels. What happens when an impulse reaches the pre-synaptic knob?

options.text_md: No neurotransmitter is released at all.
The post-synaptic neuron fires more strongly than usual.
Neurotransmitter is released but cannot generate a new potential in the post-synaptic neuron.
The impulse jumps across as an electric current instead.

questions.solution_md: Ions enter only when neurotransmitter binds receptors and opens ion channels; with receptors blocked, no new potential is generated — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The new potential generated in a post-synaptic neuron after neurotransmitter binding may be

options.text_md: always equal to the resting potential

questions.solution_md: The new potential developed in the post-synaptic neuron may be either excitatory or inhibitory — option (b).

questions.stem_md: After opening the skull, a neurosurgeon must pass through each cranial meninx in turn to reach the brain tissue. In which order will she meet them?

options.text_md: Pia mater, then arachnoid, then dura mater
Arachnoid, then dura mater, then pia mater
Dura mater, then arachnoid, then pia mater
Dura mater, then pia mater, then arachnoid

questions.solution_md: The outer layer is the dura mater, the very thin middle layer the arachnoid, and the inner layer, in contact with brain tissue, the pia mater — option (c).

questions.stem_md: To control very severe seizures, surgeons sometimes cut the broad tract of nerve fibres through which the two cerebral hemispheres communicate. Which structure is cut?
questions.solution_md: The corpus callosum is the tract of nerve fibres connecting the left and right cerebral hemispheres — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The cerebral cortex appears grey mainly because

questions.stem_md: Explain how a nerve impulse is generated and conducted along an axon. Include the resting potential, depolarisation, conduction to the next site and repolarisation.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Resting potential.** Ion channels in the axonal membrane are selectively permeable. At rest the membrane is **more permeable to K⁺** and nearly **impermeable to Na⁺** and to the negatively charged proteins of the axoplasm. The axoplasm has **high K⁺** and **low Na⁺**; the fluid outside has **low K⁺** and **high Na⁺**. The **sodium–potassium pump** moves **3 Na⁺ out for 2 K⁺ in**. The outer surface is therefore **positive** and the inner **negative**: the membrane is **polarised**, and this potential difference is the resting potential.

**Depolarisation.** When a stimulus is applied at a site A, the membrane there becomes **freely permeable to Na⁺**. A rapid **influx of Na⁺** reverses the polarity: the outer surface becomes negative and the inner positive. This is the **action potential**, or nerve impulse.

**Conduction.** At the adjacent site B the inner surface is still negative, so **current flows on the inner surface from A to B** and on the outer surface from B to A. B is depolarised and an action potential is generated there. The sequence is repeated along the length of the axon.

**Repolarisation.** The rise in Na⁺ permeability is extremely short-lived; it is quickly followed by a rise in **K⁺ permeability**. K⁺ diffuses out and the **resting potential is restored**, so the fibre is ready to respond to further stimulation.

questions.solution_md: Resting, depolarisation, conduction, repolarisation.

questions.stem_md: Describe the structure of a neuron. Classify neurons by the number of their processes, distinguish myelinated from non-myelinated fibres, and explain how an impulse passes to the next neuron at a chemical synapse.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Structure.** A neuron has a **cell body**, **dendrites** and an **axon**. The cell body contains cytoplasm with typical organelles and **Nissl’s granules**. **Dendrites** are short, repeatedly branched fibres, also with Nissl’s granules, that carry impulses **towards** the cell body. The **axon** is a long fibre whose distal end is branched; each branch ends in a bulb-like **synaptic knob** with **synaptic vesicles** containing **neurotransmitters**. Axons carry impulses **away** from the cell body.

**Types.** **Multipolar** neurons (one axon, two or more dendrites) occur in the cerebral cortex; **bipolar** (one axon, one dendrite) in the retina of the eye; **unipolar** (one axon only) usually in the embryonic stage.

**Fibres.** In **myelinated** fibres, **Schwann cells** form a **myelin sheath** with **nodes of Ranvier** between adjacent sheaths; these occur in spinal and cranial nerves. In **non-myelinated** fibres a Schwann cell encloses the axon without forming a sheath; these are common in the autonomous and somatic neural systems.

**Chemical synapse.** An impulse at the axon terminal makes the vesicles fuse with the membrane and release neurotransmitters into the **synaptic cleft**. They bind **receptors** on the post-synaptic membrane, opening **ion channels**; the entry of ions can generate a new, **excitatory or inhibitory** potential.

questions.solution_md: Structure, types, fibres, synapse.

questions.stem_md: Describe the protection, parts and functions of the human brain, organised as forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Protection.** The brain lies in the **skull** and is covered by three cranial **meninges**: the outer **dura mater**, the very thin middle **arachnoid** and the inner **pia mater**, in contact with brain tissue.

**Forebrain.** The **cerebrum**, the major part, is divided by a deep cleft into **left and right hemispheres**, joined by the **corpus callosum**. Its folded **cerebral cortex** is **grey matter**, where neuron cell bodies are concentrated; it has **motor**, **sensory** and **association areas** (intersensory associations, memory, communication). Myelinated tracts inside form **white matter**. The cerebrum wraps the **thalamus**, a coordinating centre for sensory and motor signalling. The **hypothalamus** at its base controls **body temperature** and **eating and drinking** and secretes hypothalamic hormones. With the **limbic system** (amygdala, hippocampus) it regulates sexual behaviour, emotions and motivation.

**Midbrain.** It lies between the thalamus or hypothalamus and the pons; the **cerebral aqueduct** passes through it, and its dorsal part has the four **corpora quadrigemina**.

**Hindbrain.** The **pons** has fibre tracts linking brain regions; the **cerebellum** has a very convoluted surface that gives space for many more neurons; the **medulla**, joined to the spinal cord, controls **respiration**, **cardiovascular reflexes** and **gastric secretions**. The midbrain, pons and medulla form the **brain stem**.

questions.solution_md: Protection and three regions.

questions.stem_md: A doctor taps just below a patient’s knee cap and the lower leg kicks forward. Explain this response as a reflex action, tracing the reflex arc, and explain why such reflexes are useful and why doctors test them.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Reflex action.** The kick is a **reflex action**: an **involuntary** response to a peripheral stimulus, made without conscious effort or thought but involving a part of the **central nervous system**, here the **spinal cord**.

**Reflex arc.** The tap stretches the thigh muscle, stimulating receptors in it. An **afferent (sensory) neuron** carries the impulse from the receptor via the **dorsal nerve root** into the **spinal cord**. In the grey matter it passes across a **synapse** to an **efferent (motor) neuron**. The efferent neuron carries the impulse back to the **effector**, the thigh muscle, which contracts so the leg kicks. A reflex pathway needs **at least one afferent and one efferent neuron** in series; the knee jerk uses just these two.

**Usefulness.** Because the impulse does not have to travel to the brain and back, and crosses very few synapses, reflexes are **fast and automatic**. Withdrawal reflexes, for example, pull a hand away from a hot object before damage is done.

**Why doctors test it.** A normal knee jerk shows that the **receptor, afferent neuron, spinal cord segment, efferent neuron and muscle** are all working. A missing or abnormal response points to damage somewhere along the arc.

questions.solution_md: Reflex, arc, usefulness, testing.

marking_scheme.step: Afferent, dorsal root, spinal cord, synapse

questions.stem_md: A student writes: “Every response of the human body is decided by the cerebrum.” Evaluate this statement using your knowledge of the divisions of the neural system, the roles of the hypothalamus and medulla, and reflex action.

answer.model_answer_md:
**What is right.** The **cerebrum** is the major part of the brain. Its cortex has **motor areas** that control voluntary movement, **sensory areas** and **association areas** for memory, communication and intersensory association. Conscious, voluntary responses are indeed directed from here, through the **somatic neural system** to skeletal muscles.

**What is wrong.** Many responses are not decided by the cerebrum.
- The **autonomic neural system**, with its **sympathetic** and **parasympathetic** divisions, relays impulses from the CNS to the **involuntary organs and smooth muscles** without conscious control.
- The **hypothalamus** controls **body temperature** and the urge to **eat and drink**, and secretes hormones; with the **limbic system** it shapes emotions and motivation.
- The **medulla** contains centres for **respiration**, **cardiovascular reflexes** and **gastric secretions**, which go on even during sleep.
- **Reflex actions**, such as the knee jerk or withdrawing from a hot object, are **involuntary**: the arc of afferent neuron, spinal cord and efferent neuron produces the response **without conscious thought** in the cerebrum.

**Judgement.** The statement is **too broad**. The cerebrum decides voluntary and conscious responses, but vital involuntary functions are run by the hypothalamus, medulla and autonomic system, and reflexes are handled at the level of the spinal cord.

questions.solution_md: Partly true; many responses bypass the cerebrum.

marking_scheme.step: Role of the cerebrum in voluntary responses

A scan showed swelling in the lowest part of the brain, where it joins the spinal cord, and bruising of the membranes covering the brain at the back.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (c) medulla oblongata

**(b)** (a) pia mater

**(c)** (i) The brain stem is formed by the **midbrain**, **pons** and **medulla oblongata**. It **connects the brain with the spinal cord**, and the medulla contains centres for **respiration** and **cardiovascular reflexes**, so damage here can stop vital functions.

**OR** (ii) Thinking, speech and memory depend on the **cerebral cortex** of the **cerebrum**, with its **association areas**, which lies in the forebrain far from the injured site. The **medulla** controls vital involuntary functions, so its injury disturbed **breathing and heart rate** but not thought.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** The medulla joins the spinal cord and controls respiration and cardiovascular reflexes — option (c).

**(b)** The pia mater is the inner meninx, in contact with the brain tissue — option (a).

**(c)** (i) Three parts; vital centres.

(ii) Cortex spared; medulla injured.

questions.passage_md: During a medical check-up, a doctor tapped the tendon just below a student’s knee cap with a rubber hammer, and the lower leg kicked forward at once. In this student the afferent and efferent neurons of the reflex are each about 0.6 m long and conduct at about 50 m per second; the single synapse in the spinal cord adds a delay of about 0.5 ms.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (a) a reflex action

**(b)** 24.5 ms

**(c)** (i) The tap stimulates a **receptor** in the thigh muscle. The **afferent neuron** carries the impulse via the **dorsal nerve root** into the **spinal cord**. It crosses a synapse to the **efferent neuron**, which carries it to the **effector**, the thigh muscle, which contracts.

**OR** (ii) The fault is probably in the **afferent neuron or dorsal nerve root**, or in the **receptor** or the synapse in the spinal cord. Voluntary movement shows the **efferent pathway and muscle** work, so the **reflex arc** must be broken on the incoming side.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** It is an involuntary response to a peripheral stimulus, without conscious effort — a reflex action — option (a).

**(b)** Conduction $= \dfrac{0.6 + 0.6}{50} \times 1000 = 24$ ms; total $= 24 + 0.5 = 24.5$ ms.

**(c)** (i) Receptor, afferent, spinal cord, efferent, effector.

(ii) Afferent side of the arc.
